Subject: Initial traffic & capacity needs for EdgeOps private deployment

Hi Nikhil,

Thanks for taking this on. We're evaluating Redwood's private deployment for a multi-tenant inference product we'll host in our colo racks. A few high-level numbers to start the sizing convo:

- Sustained throughput target: ~5,000 tokens/sec (aggregate across clients)
- Peak burst: up to ~12,000 tokens/sec for short windows (~5–10 minutes)
- Average response payload: ~120 tokens (mean), 95th pct ~320 tokens
- Latency target: p95 < 250ms for streaming/generative requests
- Model family: adopter plan is a 70B decoder-style model; we'll likely run a 4-bit quantized variant in prod

Questions for Redwood:
1) Recommended GPU topology (type + count) for sustained + burst with reasonable headroom?
2) Network requirements (egress, rack cross-connect, MTU) for KV cache and batching without destabilizing bursts
3) Warmup/cold-start behavior for KV cache; how much transient extra capacity should we plan for?
4) Best way to estimate autoscale thresholds for an on-prem pool (we don't want noisy scaling)

I've attached our procurement SLA and a small sample traffic trace. Can we set a 90-minute workshop next week to go through a sizing run and a network checklist?

Thanks,
Miguel

Miguel — thanks for the detail, that helps a lot. We can definitely run a workshop; how does next Tuesday (Nov 10) 10:00am PT look? I'll invite the right engineers.

High-level answers to your numbered items so we can calibrate the workshop:

1) GPU topology: we'll propose a baseline made of homogenous nodes for operational simplicity, plus a small heterogeneous pool for burst optimizations. Ballpark math: convert tokens/sec -> requests/sec by dividing by avg tokens/request: 5,000 / 120 ≈ 42 rps sustained. Peak 12k -> 100 rps.

2) Network: KV cache sync and model chunk transfer benefit from low-latency fabric. Plan for 25–40 Gbps per GPU node (depending on model size and embedding transfer pattern); jumbo frames and MTU tuning help.

3) Warmup: KV cache cold-warm windows can multiply token generation cost for the initial minutes — plan an extra 30–50% transient capacity or use pre-warm runs if predictable traffic exists.

4) Autoscale: use queue-depth + observed batch-size heuristics rather than simple CPU/RAM triggers. Set min replicas based on steady-state, and add a pre-warmed burst pool for quick absorption.

I'll leave the detailed math and orchestration notes to Lauren and Dev — copying them in. Please attach any traffic percentiles (P50/P95/P99) and a sample payload set ahead of the workshop.

Best,

Miguel / team — adding concrete sizing math and a few recommendations we find useful on private pools. TL;DR: translate tokens -> req/s -> effective tokens/s per GPU, then add buffer for warmup, autoscale latency, and maintenance.

Sizing formula (simplified):
- sustained_tokens_per_sec = T_s (5,000)
- avg_tokens_per_req = t_avg (120)
- sustained_req_s = T_s / t_avg → 5,000 / 120 ≈ 41.7 rps
- effective_tokens_per_gpu = G_eff (depends on model + quantization + batching). For a 70B decoder quantized to 4-bit with efficient batching and warmed KV cache we see anywhere from 300–600 tokens/sec per high-end GPU in our fleets (varies by kernel set and sequence length).
- required_gpus = ceil(T_s / G_eff)

Example scenarios: (illustrative)
- Conservative G_eff = 300 -> required_gpus = ceil(5000/300) = 17 GPUs
- Optimistic G_eff = 500 -> required_gpus = ceil(5000/500) = 10 GPUs

Add operational buffers:
- Headroom for autoscale + burst (40% recommended) -> 14–24 GPUs in the two scenarios above
- Warmup multiplier (30% transients) -> plan short-term extra capacity or pre-warming strategy

Networking notes:
- KV cache traffic tends to be small requests but high QPS; prefer a dedicated 10–25Gbps per rack for control/kv traffic and 25–100Gbps fabric for model weights/chunk transfer depending on model shard size.
- Latency-sensitive workloads benefit from colocating storage for model shards (NVMe on host or NVMeoF) to avoid connector cross-talk.

Autoscale guidance:
- Maintain a small pre-warmed pool (10–20% of baseline) to absorb sudden bursts without triggering expensive cold starts.
- Autoscale triggers: high queue depth + sustained increase in average batch size; scale down with hysteresis (10–15m cool-down).

Operational suggestions:
- Reserve spare GPUs for rolling upgrades and evacuation (10% runway).
- Instrument: tokens/s per GPU, end-to-end p95 latency, queue depth, batch-size distribution, model cache hit ratio.

I'll prepare a short worksheet with the above calculations and a few GPU-performance baselines we use internally. Attaching a capacity calculator workbook (runbook-capacity-calc.xlsx) and our quantization profile doc.

— Lauren

Quick operational checklist from an on-prem deployment perspective (adds to Lauren's math):

- Node sizing: prefer 4–8 GPUs per server for manageable failure domains. Example: 4x H100 or 8x A40 depending on customer preference/cost.
- Rack planning: budget 1.2–1.5x network capacity vs steady-state model shard transfer to avoid saturation during rolling restarts.
- Storage: use local NVMe for model shard cache; fall back to NFS/S3 for cold objects. NVMeoF helps if you need cross-node sharing but adds network load.
- Power/cooling: margin for peak sustained CPU/GPU usage when calculating PDU and cooling (we've seen 20–30% higher draw during bursts due to host CPU and NVMe activity).
- Deployment patterns: start with a minimum replicated pool sized to absorb steady-state plus a pre-warmed burst pool (can be smaller, heterogeneous GPUs).

Instrumentation (must-haves):
- Per-GPU tokens/s, GPU memory utilization, batch-size histogram, queue depth, p95/p99 latency, cache hit rate, kernel fallback rates (quantization -> fallback to fp16), and node-level health.

Runbook excerpts (attached):
- Warmup script: replay a sampled trace for the first 10 minutes of a rollout to pre-populate KV cache.
- Failover: if a node goes offline, route new requests to dedicated fallback pool with degraded latency SLA; drain and rebuild offline node while maintaining minimum healthy replicas.

I'll bring a draft runbook and the sample kube + systemd unit snippets to the workshop.
